claim: Nhlh2 is enriched in Kiss1 neurons of the arcuate nucleus in adult mice
source: Using a previously described database of ARH transcripts from 20,921 cells from adult wild-type (WT) male and female mice (Campbell et al., 2017), we identified the bHLH TF Nhlh2, as a highly enriched transcript in arcuate Kiss1 neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by Drop-Seq analysis of ARH transcripts from adult mice, which is experimental data from the Campbell et al., 2017 database.

claim: 71% of Kiss1ARH neurons in adult wild-type males co-express Nhlh2
source: In situ hybridization, though RNAscope assay of Kiss1 and Nhlh2 confirmed this co-expression in 71% of Kiss1ARH neurons of adult WT males (Figure 1A,D)
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A,D.

claim: NHLH2 has several binding sites in the Kiss1 and Tac2/3 5' regulatory regions
source: JASPAR analysis revealed several binding sites for NHLH2 in the Kiss1 and Tac2 (neurokinin B) 5′ regulatory regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by JASPAR computational analysis of promoter regions.

claim: The Tac2/3 genes contain approximately 1 NHLH2 binding site every 80 nucleotides
source: Moreover, the Tac2/3 genes seemed more enriched at an average of 1 site every 80 nt while the Kiss1 promoter region contained 1 site every 150 nt (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by JASPAR analysis results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Kiss1 promoter region contains approximately 1 NHLH2 binding site every 150 nucleotides
source: Moreover, the Tac2/3 genes seemed more enriched at an average of 1 site every 80 nt while the Kiss1 promoter region contained 1 site every 150 nt (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by JASPAR analysis results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: NHLH2 stimulates human KISS1 promoter activity up to 6-fold
source: Transfection of either promoter resulted in increased luciferase activity compared with the empty pGL2 vector, this activity was significantly enhanced by NHLH2 co-expression, reaching a 6-fold and a 20-fold increase in KISS1 and TAC3 promoter activity, respectively, at the highest NHLH2 concentration (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: NHLH2 stimulates human TAC3 promoter activity up to 20-fold
source: Transfection of either promoter resulted in increased luciferase activity compared with the empty pGL2 vector, this activity was significantly enhanced by NHLH2 co-expression, reaching a 6-fold and a 20-fold increase in KISS1 and TAC3 promoter activity, respectively, at the highest NHLH2 concentration (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The TAC3 promoter is more sensitive to NHLH2 stimulation than the KISS1 promoter
source: Interestingly, the TAC3 promoter was more sensitive to NHLH2 stimulation, since the promoter was activated even at the lowest doses (Figure 2D), in line with the JASPAR analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2D and is consistent with JASPAR analysis.

claim: NHLH2 directly interacts with the Kiss1 and Tac3 immediate 5'-regulatory regions
source: Furthermore, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays showed that NHLH2 directly interacts with the Kiss1 and Tac3 immediate 5′-regulatory regions, as opposed to an enhancer site located ~3 kb upstream of the Kiss1 TSS, where no binding sites were detected (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Nhlh2 expression in the mediobasal hypothalamus decreases significantly from early juvenile onwards in males
source: Nhlh2 expression decreased significantly from early juvenile onwards in males and late juvenile in females (Figure 3B and D)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Nhlh2 expression in the mediobasal hypothalamus decreases significantly from late juvenile onwards in females
source: Nhlh2 expression decreased significantly from early juvenile onwards in males and late juvenile in females (Figure 3B and D)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Kiss1 expression in the mediobasal hypothalamus does not change significantly during postnatal development in males
source: Kiss1 expression in the MBH of male (Figure 3A) and female (Figure 3C) mice did not experience any significant change in expression, as previously described (Gill et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A and is consistent with previous literature (Gill et al., 2012).

claim: Kiss1 expression in the mediobasal hypothalamus does not change significantly during postnatal development in females
source: Kiss1 expression in the MBH of male (Figure 3A) and female (Figure 3C) mice did not experience any significant change in expression, as previously described (Gill et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C and is consistent with previous literature (Gill et al., 2012).

claim: Female Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice display normal timing of puberty onset
source: Female Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice displayed normal timing of puberty onset, determined through the day of vaginal opening (VO) and first estrus (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by puberty monitoring data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Female Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice have disrupted estrous cycles with more time in diestrus and less time in estrus
source: Further examination of the estrous cycles for 30 days after VO revealed a significant disruption in estrous cyclicity, with Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice spending more time in diestrus and less time in estrus (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by estrous cycle monitoring data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Female Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice have normal LH surge magnitude
source: This experiment revealed a similar magnitude of the LH surge in both groups (Figure 4G), indicating that Nhlh2 in Kiss1 neurons is not necessary for the generation of the preovulatory LH surge in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by LH surge induction protocol data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Nhlh2 in Kiss1 neurons is not necessary for the generation of the preovulatory LH surge in mice
source: This experiment revealed a similar magnitude of the LH surge in both groups (Figure 4G), indicating that Nhlh2 in Kiss1 neurons is not necessary for the generation of the preovulatory LH surge in mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the LH surge data showing no difference between control and Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice.

claim: Male Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice have delayed puberty onset
source: In males, the specific deletion of Nhlh2 from Kiss1 neurons led to a significant delay in puberty onset, as observed by preputial separation (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by preputial separation monitoring data shown in Figure 4H,I.

claim: Male Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice have slightly higher body weight at the time of puberty onset than controls
source: Due to the older age, the body weight (BW) at the time of puberty onset in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl males was slightly higher than in controls (Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Overall body weight throughout development does not differ between Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl and control mice in either sex under regular chow diet
source: However, the overall BW throughout development did not change between genotypes in either sex during 130 days of study postnatally under regular chow diet (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight monitoring data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: High-fat diet does not reveal any significant difference in body weight between Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl and control mice
source: This metabolic challenge did not reveal any significant difference in BW between groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight data during HFD shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice retain normal fertility compared to controls
source: Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice retained normal fertility compared to the control as evidenced by their parturition latency, number of pups per litter, and number of litters in 3 months (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fertility assessment data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Male Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice present a variable phenotype with a fraction showing absent or severely reduced fertility
source: However, male Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice presented a variable phenotype with a fraction of them showing absent or severely reduced fertility (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fertility assessment data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Testes of Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl males show mature sperm
source: Testes of Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl males show mature sperm, and ovaries of Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl females presented similar numbers of growing follicles and corpora lutea (CL) as controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ovaries of Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl females present similar numbers of growing follicles and corpora lutea as controls
source: Testes of Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl males show mature sperm, and ovaries of Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl females presented similar numbers of growing follicles and corpora lutea (CL) as controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kiss1 expression is significantly decreased in the mediobasal hypothalamus of male Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice
source: Expression analysis of the KNDy genes revealed a significant decrease in the expression of Kiss1 in the MBH of male and female Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl, which was further observed by RNAscope (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and RNAscope data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Kiss1 expression is significantly decreased in the mediobasal hypothalamus of female Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice
source: Expression analysis of the KNDy genes revealed a significant decrease in the expression of Kiss1 in the MBH of male and female Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl, which was further observed by RNAscope (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and RNAscope data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Tac2 and Pdyn expression remain similar to controls in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl males
source: Interestingly, while the expression of the rest of the KNDy genes (Tac2 and Pdyn) remained similar to controls in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl males (Figure 6A)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Tac2 and Pdyn expression are significantly decreased in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl females
source: there was a significant decrease in the expression of both genes in females (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Tacr3 expression shows a modest but significant increase in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl males
source: The NKB receptor (Tacr3) showed a modest but significant increase in the expression in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl males, while it remained unchanged in females.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: Tacr3 expression remains unchanged in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl females
source: The NKB receptor (Tacr3) showed a modest but significant increase in the expression in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl males, while it remained unchanged in females.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: Central administration of kisspeptin-10 induces similar LH responses in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl and control males
source: Despite the decrease in Kiss1, the central administration of kisspeptin-10 (Kp-10; 50 pmol) or the NK3R agonist senktide (600 pmol) in males induced similar responses in terms of LH release in both genotypes (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by LH measurement data after Kp-10 administration shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Central administration of senktide induces similar LH responses in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl and control males
source: Despite the decrease in Kiss1, the central administration of kisspeptin-10 (Kp-10; 50 pmol) or the NK3R agonist senktide (600 pmol) in males induced similar responses in terms of LH release in both genotypes (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by LH measurement data after senktide administration shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The response of males to gonadectomy after 10 days is similar between Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl and control groups
source: Moreover, the response of males to gonadectomy (GDX) after 10 days was also similar between both groups (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by LH measurement data after gonadectomy shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice show a significantly faster reduction in circulating LH levels during 24-hour fasting than controls
source: This protocol led to a significantly faster reduction in circulating LH levels in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice than in Nhlh2fl/fl controls (Figure 7D)
evidence: The claim is supported by LH measurement data during fasting shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice are more sensitive to decreasing levels of energy reserves
source: This protocol led to a significantly faster reduction in circulating LH levels in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice than in Nhlh2fl/fl controls (Figure 7D), suggesting that these mice are more sensitive to decreasing levels of energy reserves.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the faster LH reduction during fasting in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice.

claim: The response to refeeding is similar in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl and control mice
source: However, the response to refeeding was similar in both groups, indicating that metabolic cues can still activate Kiss1 neurons in an Nhlh2-independent manner within Kiss1 neurons or indirectly through other neurons, for example, POMC.
evidence: The claim is supported by LH measurement data during refeeding.

claim: Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice display a significantly lower LH response to leptin administration after overnight fasting compared to controls
source: The results showed that Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice displayed a significantly lower response to leptin compared to controls (Figure 7E)
evidence: The claim is supported by LH measurement data after leptin administration shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Nhlh2 serves as a mechanism for Kiss1 neurons to respond to leptin action
source: The results showed that Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice displayed a significantly lower response to leptin compared to controls (Figure 7E), thus supporting the contention that Nhlh2 serves as a mechanism for Kiss1 neurons to respond to leptin action, likely through its interaction with STAT3 (AL_Rayyan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the impaired leptin response in Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice and supported by previous literature on Nhlh2/STAT3 interaction.

claim: Nhlh2 likely interacts with STAT3 in the leptin signaling pathway
source: The results showed that Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice displayed a significantly lower response to leptin compared to controls (Figure 7E), thus supporting the contention that Nhlh2 serves as a mechanism for Kiss1 neurons to respond to leptin action, likely through its interaction with STAT3 (AL_Rayyan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by previous literature (AL_Rayyan et al., 2014) and the leptin response data.

claim: Hypothalamic Kiss1 neurons control gonadotropin-releasing hormone release through the secretion of kisspeptin
source: Hypothalamic Kiss1 neurons control gonadotropin-releasing hormone release through the secretion of kisspeptin.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation (Pinilla et al., 2012) in the introduction.

claim: Kisspeptins act directly on gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons
source: Hypothalamic Kiss1 neurons secrete kisspeptins (Pinilla et al., 2012), which act directly on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons (Irwig et al., 2004) to stimulate GnRH release.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Irwig et al., 2004.

claim: The absence of proper kisspeptin signaling leads to absent or delayed puberty, hypogonadism, and infertility
source: The absence of proper kisspeptin signaling leads to absent or delayed puberty, hypogonadism, and infertility (de Roux et al., 2003; Seminara et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to de Roux et al., 2003 and Seminara et al., 2003.

claim: Kiss1 neurons are mainly found in the arcuate nucleus and the anteroventral periventricular nucleus
source: Kiss1 neurons are mainly found in two distinct hypothalamic nuclei, the arcuate nucleus (ARH) and the anteroventral periventricular nucleus (AVPV/PeN) (Pinilla et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pinilla et al., 2012.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons mediate the pulsatile release of GnRH
source: Kiss1ARH neurons mediate the pulsatile release of GnRH (Clarkson et al., 2017; Navarro et al., 2009; Wakabayashi et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clarkson et al., 2017; Navarro et al., 2009; Wakabayashi et al., 2010.

claim: Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons are almost exclusive to the female brain and control the surge-like release of GnRH
source: while Kiss1AVPV/PeN are almost exclusive to the female brain and control the surge-like release of GnRH (Caraty et al., 2007; Sébert et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Caraty et al., 2007 and Sébert et al., 2010.

claim: Pulsatile GnRH release increases at the end of the juvenile period, determining the onset of puberty
source: Pulsatile GnRH release increases at the end of the juvenile period, determining the onset of puberty and the transition into adulthood (Ojeda et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ojeda et al., 2010.

claim: The onset of puberty is largely dependent on the activation of Kiss1 neurons
source: This process is largely dependent on the activation of Kiss1 neurons, in part, through the autosynaptic excitatory action of neurokinin B (NKB) (Garcia et al., 2017; Gill et al., 2012; Navarro et al., 2012a; Ruiz-Pino et al., 2012) and the inhibitory action of dynorphin through an autosynaptic alternation process that creates the kisspeptin pulse generator (Clarkson et al., 2017; Navarro et al., 2009; Plant, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing the role of Kiss1 neurons in puberty onset.

claim: Neurokinin B has an autosynaptic excitatory action on Kiss1 neurons
source: This process is largely dependent on the activation of Kiss1 neurons, in part, through the autosynaptic excitatory action of neurokinin B (NKB) (Garcia et al., 2017; Gill et al., 2012; Navarro et al., 2012a; Ruiz-Pino et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Garcia et al., 2017; Gill et al., 2012; Navarro et al., 2012a; Ruiz-Pino et al., 2012.

claim: Dynorphin has an inhibitory action on Kiss1 neurons through an autosynaptic alternation process
source: and the inhibitory action of dynorphin through an autosynaptic alternation process that creates the kisspeptin pulse generator (Clarkson et al., 2017; Navarro et al., 2009; Plant, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clarkson et al., 2017; Navarro et al., 2009; Plant, 2019.

claim: Energy balance is a critical component in the control of puberty onset and maintenance of reproductive function
source: Energy balance is a critical component in the control of puberty onset and maintenance of reproductive function in adulthood (Navarro, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Navarro, 2020.

claim: Deficient energy reserves are often associated with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea
source: Deficient energy reserves are often associated with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (Laughlin et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Laughlin et al., 1998.

claim: AgRP and neuropeptide Y directly inhibit Kiss1 neurons under energetic deficit
source: For example, the hunger signals agouti-related peptide (AgRP) and neuropeptide Y, produced in hypothalamic AgRP neurons, directly inhibit Kiss1 neurons under energetic deficit (Padilla et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Padilla et al., 2017.

claim: AgRP neurons express the leptin receptor
source: AgRP neurons, as well as Kiss1 neurons themselves, express the leptin receptor (Lepr) and are therefore direct targets of leptin, which is produced in the adipose tissue as a direct measure of the level of fat reserves (Backholer et al., 2010; Cravo et al., 2013; Egan et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2006; True et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Backholer et al., 2010; Cravo et al., 2013; Egan et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2006; True et al., 2011.

claim: Kiss1 neurons express the leptin receptor
source: AgRP neurons, as well as Kiss1 neurons themselves, express the leptin receptor (Lepr) and are therefore direct targets of leptin, which is produced in the adipose tissue as a direct measure of the level of fat reserves (Backholer et al., 2010; Cravo et al., 2013; Egan et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2006; True et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Backholer et al., 2010; Cravo et al., 2013; Egan et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2006; True et al., 2011.

claim: Leptin is produced in the adipose tissue as a direct measure of the level of fat reserves
source: AgRP neurons, as well as Kiss1 neurons themselves, express the leptin receptor (Lepr) and are therefore direct targets of leptin, which is produced in the adipose tissue as a direct measure of the level of fat reserves (Backholer et al., 2010; Cravo et al., 2013; Egan et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2006; True et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: Deficient leptin signaling leads to obesity and infertility in ob/ob or db/db mice
source: Deficient leptin signaling, as occurs in ob/ob or db/db mice, leads to obesity and infertility (Donato et al., 2011b; Leshan et al., 2006; Navarro and Kaiser, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Donato et al., 2011b; Leshan et al., 2006; Navarro and Kaiser, 2013.

claim: The main control of metabolic and reproductive functions by leptin requires GABAergic neurons
source: Evidence from our lab and others indicate that the main control of both functions by leptin requires GABAergic neurons (Martin et al., 2014; Vong et al., 2011; Zuure et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martin et al., 2014; Vong et al., 2011; Zuure et al., 2013.

claim: Deletion of Lepr from glutamatergic neurons leads to a subtle metabolic and reproductive phenotype
source: while the deletion of Lepr from glutamatergic neurons leads to a subtle metabolic and reproductive phenotype (Martin et al., 2014; Vong et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martin et al., 2014; Vong et al., 2011.

claim: Kiss1 neurons of the ARH are mostly glutamatergic
source: Interestingly, Kiss1 neurons of the ARH are mostly glutamatergic (Nestor et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nestor et al., 2016.

claim: Deletion of Lepr from Kiss1 neurons does not prevent fertility in mice
source: and the deletion of Lepr from Kiss1 neurons does not prevent fertility in mice (Cravo et al., 2013; Donato et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cravo et al., 2013; Donato et al., 2011a.

claim: Leptin plays its primary reproductive role upstream of Kiss1 neurons
source: These data suggest that leptin plays its primary reproductive role upstream of Kiss1 neurons and that the expression of Lepr in these neurons is limited to a modulatory role, likely in the acute regulation of kisspeptin release under specific metabolic conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that deletion of Lepr from Kiss1 neurons does not prevent fertility.

claim: Insulin can directly act on Kiss1 neurons
source: In addition to leptin, other peripheral factors that signal energetic state can directly act on Kiss1 neurons as well, such as insulin (Qiu et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Qiu et al., 2015.

claim: Kiss1 neurons are a nodal target for metabolic cues
source: In addition to leptin, other peripheral factors that signal energetic state can directly act on Kiss1 neurons as well, such as insulin (Qiu et al., 2015), suggesting that Kiss1 neurons are a nodal target for metabolic cues (Navarro, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Qiu et al., 2015 and Navarro, 2020.

claim: Conditions of negative energy balance rapidly and potently inhibit the reproductive axis
source: Conditions of negative energy balance rapidly and potently inhibit the reproductive axis, preventing or delaying puberty onset and fertility (Navarro, 2020; Castellano et al., 2011; Luque et al., 2007; Roa et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Navarro, 2020; Castellano et al., 2011; Luque et al., 2007; Roa et al., 2008.

claim: Upon restoration of energy reserves, kisspeptin pulses resume and the reproductive axis becomes reactivated
source: Upon restoration of energy reserves, kisspeptin pulses resume and the reproductive axis becomes reactivated (Navarro, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Navarro, 2020.

claim: SP-1 and AP-2α are activators of the Kiss1 promoter in cancer cell lines
source: In vitro studies in cancer cell lines have identified SP-1 and AP-2α as activators of the Kiss1 promoter (Mitchell et al., 2006; Mitchell et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 2006; Mitchell et al., 2007.

claim: TTF1 and CUX1-p200 are potential enhancers of Kiss1 transcription in humans
source: while in vivo only TTF1 and CUX1-p200 in the human (Mueller et al., 2011), and Tbx3 and Crtc1 in the mouse (Sanz et al., 2015; Altarejos et al., 2008), have been identified as potential enhancers of Kiss1 transcription
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mueller et al., 2011.

claim: Tbx3 and Crtc1 are potential enhancers of Kiss1 transcription in mice
source: while in vivo only TTF1 and CUX1-p200 in the human (Mueller et al., 2011), and Tbx3 and Crtc1 in the mouse (Sanz et al., 2015; Altarejos et al., 2008), have been identified as potential enhancers of Kiss1 transcription
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sanz et al., 2015; Altarejos et al., 2008.

claim: Crtc1 is involved in the transcriptional regulation of Kiss1 by metabolic cues
source: Of these TFs, only Crtc1 (Altarejos et al., 2008) has been involved in the transcriptional regulation of Kiss1 by metabolic cues
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Altarejos et al., 2008.

claim: Nhlh2 is a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor
source: we have identified the bHLH (Jones, 2004) TF Nhlh2
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jones, 2004.

claim: Nhlh2 is the most enriched transcript in Kiss1 neurons ahead of Tac2 and Pdyn
source: Among those, Nhlh2 appeared as the gene that strongly marked Kiss1 neurons, being the most enriched transcript in these neurons ahead of the KNDy co-transmitters Tac2 and Pdyn (Lehman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by Drop-Seq analysis data and citation to Lehman et al., 2010.

claim: Nhlh2 is highly expressed in Kiss1 neurons from the time of their initial development during the embryonic phase
source: Nhlh2 is highly expressed in Kiss1 neurons from the time of their initial development during the embryonic phase (Huisman et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Huisman et al., 2019.

claim: Nhlh2 has been shown to be involved in the development of the brain, including GnRH and POMC neurons
source: Nhlh2 has been shown to be involved in the development of the brain, including GnRH and POMC neurons (Schmid et al., 2013; Cogliati et al., 2007; Fox et al., 2007; Vella et al., 2007; Good et al., 1997; Johnson et al., 2004; Krüger et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Nhlh2 KO male mice are infertile, presenting small penises at weaning, cryptorchidism, and no signs of puberty
source: Nhlh2 KO male mice are infertile, presenting small penises at weaning, cryptorchidism, and no signs of puberty (Good et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Good et al., 1997.

claim: Nhlh2 KO females are hypogonadal, displaying small ovaries, thread-like uteri, delayed puberty onset, and irregular cycles when reared alone
source: In the same vein, Nhlh2 KO females are hypogonadal, displaying small ovaries, thread-like uteri, delayed puberty onset (first estrus), and irregular cycles when reared alone, but they are fertile when reared in the presence of males (Cogliati et al., 2007; Good et al., 1997; Johnson et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cogliati et al., 2007; Good et al., 1997; Johnson et al., 2004.

claim: Nhlh2 KO females are fertile when reared in the presence of males
source: In the same vein, Nhlh2 KO females are hypogonadal, displaying small ovaries, thread-like uteri, delayed puberty onset (first estrus), and irregular cycles when reared alone, but they are fertile when reared in the presence of males (Cogliati et al., 2007; Good et al., 1997; Johnson et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cogliati et al., 2007; Good et al., 1997; Johnson et al., 2004.

claim: Nhlh2 has been implicated in the migratory process of a fraction of GnRH neurons
source: Interestingly, while Nhlh2 has been implicated in the migratory process of a fraction of GnRH neurons (Cogliati et al., 2007; Johnson et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cogliati et al., 2007; Johnson et al., 2004.

claim: Nhlh2 KO mice show large amounts of GnRH neurons in the preoptic area
source: Nhlh2 KO mice still show large amounts of GnRH neurons in the preoptic area (well above the 12% of GnRH neurons that is required for normal reproductive function; Herbison et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Herbison et al., 2008.

claim: Specific ablation of Nhlh2 from GnRH neurons using Gnrh1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice displayed normal reproductive function despite a 20% reduction in the number of GnRH neurons
source: Moreover, specific ablation of Nhlh2 from GnRH neurons using Gnrh1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl mice displayed normal reproductive function despite a 20% reduction in the number of GnRH neurons (Schmid et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schmid et al., 2013.

claim: GnRH neurons do not express Nhlh2 beyond embryonic day 18.5E
source: In addition, GnRH neurons do not express Nhlh2 beyond embryonic day 18.5E (Cogliati et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cogliati et al., 2007.

claim: 5% of kisspeptin production is sufficient to maintain reproductive capabilities
source: It has been demonstrated that 5% of kisspeptin production is sufficient to maintain reproductive capabilities (Popa et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Popa et al., 2013.

claim: Whole-body Nhlh2 KO females reared with males show normal reproductive phenotype
source: Kiss1Cre:Nhlh2fl/fl females displayed normal timing of puberty onset and fertility although their estrous cycles were disrupted under normal chow diet, resembling the phenotype of whole-body Nhlh2 KO females reared with males (Good et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Good et al., 1997.

claim: The population of Kiss1 neurons in the preoptic area is virtually absent in males
source: However, the hypothalamic Kiss1 system is sexually differentiated, and the population of Kiss1 neurons in the preoptic area (Kiss1AVPV/PeN), which is virtually absent in males (Smith et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2005.
